title: Hirsutism & the Ferriman–Gallwey score
summary: Male-pattern terminal hair growth in women: scoring with the modified Ferriman–Gallwey scale, causes (mostly PCOS or idiopathic), the tests that matter, and treatment from hair removal and the pill to specialist anti-androgens.

glance.think: A woman distressed by terminal hair on the face, chest, abdomen or back.
glance.engine: Androgen excess (ovary, adrenal, drugs) or increased follicle sensitivity to normal androgens (idiopathic).
glance.backbone: Score and record impact, check testosterone and screen for PCOS; hair removal methods and a COC; eflornithine cream has been discontinued in the UK, so check availability; specialist anti-androgens with contraception.
glance.never_miss: Rapid-onset virilisation (deep voice, clitoromegaly, testosterone >5 nmol/L): androgen-secreting tumour.

what: **Hirsutism** is excess **terminal** hair in a woman, in an **androgen-dependent (male-pattern)** distribution: upper lip, chin, jawline/sideburns, chest, abdomen, back, thighs. It differs from **hypertrichosis**, which is excess hair in a non-androgen pattern (e.g. drug-induced by ciclosporin, minoxidil or phenytoin, or paraneoplastic lanugo).
cause: The cause is increased **androgen production** (ovary, adrenal) and/or increased **follicle sensitivity**: 5α-reductase in the pilosebaceous unit converts testosterone to DHT.

list: **PCOS** (~70–80% of hirsutism); **idiopathic hirsutism** (normal androgens and ovulatory cycles, ~5–15%); idiopathic hyperandrogenaemia.

Less common causes: **non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia** (21-hydroxylase deficiency — check 17-OH-progesterone); **Cushing's**, acromegaly, hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disease; **androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumours** (rapid onset, virilisation, testosterone often >5 nmol/L); drugs (anabolic steroids, testosterone, danazol, valproate); menopause
Normal hair density varies widely with ethnicity and family. Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and South Asian women often have more terminal hair; East Asian women less.

features: The case: **dark terminal hair limited to the jawline and sideburns**, FG ≈2 in that area, **regular periods**, distress, **BMI 28**, **testosterone 1.2 nmol/L (<2)**, **androstenedione 6.5 nmol/L (<10)**. No virilisation, acne or AN is recorded.

list: **Scoring:** **9 androgen-sensitive areas** — upper lip, chin, chest, upper abdomen, lower abdomen, upper arms, thighs, upper back, lower back. Each scores **0 (no terminal hair) to 4 (frankly virile)**, for a **total of 0–36**.

**Cut-offs:** **≥8** is the traditional threshold in white and black women; Lower cut-offs (**≥4–6**) are used in some populations, e.g. East Asian women. The 2018/2023 International PCOS guideline accepts **≥4–6** depending on ethnicity; Also recognise "**patient-important hirsutism**": localised hair that distresses the patient even with a low total, as here

**Limitations:** subjective, with inter-observer variation; underestimates hair after hair removal; no extra weighting for the face (the most distressing site); does not capture distress, so pair it with a QoL measure; Its main use is to **monitor response**

**Work-up (UK — CKS hirsutism / Endocrine Society):** **History:** onset and pace, cycles, fertility, weight change, drugs (including supplements and anabolic steroids), family history; **Examination:** virilisation (clitoromegaly, deep voice, male-pattern balding, increased muscle bulk), acne, AN, Cushingoid signs, BP, BMI; **Bloods:**; **Total testosterone** (early follicular, morning) and **SHBG/free androgen index**; As indicated: **LH/FSH, prolactin, TSH, 17-OH-progesterone**; If PCOS is likely: HbA1c/OGTT and lipids; Pregnancy test; **Pelvic USS** only if PCOS criteria are uncertain. It is not needed when 2 criteria are already met, and is not used within 8 years of menarche

**Interpreting the case:** Normal androgens, regular cycles and mild localised hair are most consistent with **idiopathic (peripheral) hirsutism** or a constitutional/ethnic hair pattern; PCOS is **not excluded**: regular cycles can still be anovulatory (check mid-luteal progesterone), and ~20–30% of women with PCOS have a normal total testosterone (check SHBG/FAI); Her BMI of 28 justifies an insulin-resistance work-up (HbA1c)

management: **Therapeutic strategy for the case:** treat the patient's goals, layer treatments, and set expectations — hormonal effects take 6–12 months, and a hair cycle is about 6 months.

ol: **Lifestyle:** **weight reduction** (even 5% improves SHBG, androgens and insulin resistance) and exercise; address any PCOS/metabolic risk.

**Cosmetic/physical methods** (first-line; mostly self-funded in the UK): Shaving — it does *not* make hair thicker; Plucking, threading or waxing — risk of folliculitis and PIH; Depilatory creams (irritant) and bleaching; **Laser/IPL** — best for dark hair on light skin; **Nd:YAG** for darker skin; needs multiple sessions. NHS funding is very limited and ICB-specific, often only for severe cases or gender services; **Electrolysis** — permanent but slow; works on any hair colour

**Topical eflornithine 11.5% cream (Vaniqa):** An irreversible ornithine-decarboxylase inhibitor that slows facial hair growth. Apply twice daily; effect by 6–8 weeks; stop if no benefit at 4 months. The effect is lost about 8 weeks after stopping. Works best combined with laser; **2026 status:** NHS dm+d lists **Vaniqa as discontinued/not available** in the UK, and several ICBs (e.g. Pan Mersey, BSW) class it as **not recommended**. Check local availability before suggesting it

**Systemic hormonal therapy** (if distress persists despite ≥6 months of cosmetic measures): A **COC** is the first-line systemic option (↓ ovarian androgen, ↑ SHBG); any low-VTE COC such as a levonorgestrel pill is a reasonable start; **Co-cyprindiol** is licensed for **severe hirsutism** but carries ~1.5–2× the VTE risk (MHRA 2013); stop 3–4 cycles after control; **Anti-androgens** (spironolactone 50–200 mg/day, higher-dose cyproterone acetate, finasteride) are **off-label and specialist-advised**, need **reliable contraception** (feminisation of a male fetus), and are usually added to a COC after 6 months of inadequate response; **Higher-dose cyproterone (≥10 mg/day)** carries a dose-related **meningioma** risk (MHRA 2020) — specialist only
**Psychological support** — hirsutism has a major impact on self-.

list: **Rapid onset or progression**, **virilisation**, **testosterone >5 nmol/L** (or >2× ULN), raised DHEAS, or a pelvic/abdominal mass → **urgent endocrinology/gynaecology** for a suspected androgen-secreting tumour (NICE NG12 if there is a mass).
Features of **Cushing's**, acromegaly or hyperprolactinaemia; suspected NC-CAH; new hirsutism after the menopause.
Distress not responding to primary-care measures → endocrinology/dermatology per the local pathway.

management: Assessment, bloods, lifestyle and cosmetic advice, and **COC prescribing within contraceptive competence and UKMEC** are within IP scope. Anti-androgens, co-cyprindiol for hirsutism (formulary-dependent) and laser referral criteria follow local specialist pathways.
red_flags: Rapid onset over months, virilisation or a very high testosterone: **urgent** endocrine referral to exclude an androgen-secreting tumour.
Anti-androgens (spironolactone, cyproterone, finasteride) are teratogenic to a male fetus: effective contraception is essential.
pearls: "Hormonal treatment stops **new** hair coarsening; it doesn't remove existing hair" — so combine it with physical removal.
Shaving is safe and effective, and does not make regrowth thicker or darker.
Ask about **drugs and supplements**: testosterone gel transferred by contact with a partner, anabolic steroids, valproate; minoxidil causes hypertrichosis.
